correctness.rationale: For exactly two required volunteers the strategy gain is benefit times probability that precisely one partner contributes, minus cost, giving B x Σw_j(n_j−1)(1−x)^(n_j−2)−c. Under z=1−x it is a nonzero polynomial with at most 2m+1 monomials and thus at most 2m positive zeros by Descartes, counting multiplicity. The witness sizes R^j+1 have positive pivotality >1/(em) at p_i=R^(−i), and valleys <1/(16m) at q_i=(L R^i)^(−1), versus cost ratio 1/(4m). The log inequalities, monotonic t exp(−t), and L≥16 justify every comparison; signs at boundaries and interleaved points give 2m disjoint root intervals. The Descartes count then forces simplicity and alternating stability. A standalone program establishes an illustrative m=2 four-root instance with exact fractions, not the general theorem.

originality.rationale: A literature-led check included source papers introducing exogenous experienced group-size distributions, fixed-size threshold public goods, stochastic-order effects of variable size, and older fixed-size threshold bifurcations. The two most direct papers explicitly leave nontrivial quorum cases outside their respective analyses. Novelty remains relative to accessible texts and is subject to uninspected older literature.

value.rationale: A motivating 2012 mathematical-evolution paper identified intermediate quorum volunteer games with fluctuating group sizes as harder, and a 2016 analysis of group-size variability specifically excluded their nonconvex gain sequences from general conclusions. The proved sharp 2m law replaces single-basin expectations with exact resource-dependent control of equilibrium complexity, while explicit examples establish arbitrarily many coexisting stable cooperation frequencies. Finite support m is a natural invariant: it measures the number of ecologically distinct experienced group sizes, not a handpicked arithmetic window. Construction is extreme and does not claim empirical prevalence.
